title: Weaner group — farmed red deer: ill-thrift and scour after weaning
presentation: Forty farmed red deer calves weaned six weeks ago onto a wet lowland paddock. A third are scouring intermittently, growth rates have stalled, and one calf was found dead this morning.

stages.title: Assess the group
stages.briefing: Affected calves: rough coats, dirty hindquarters, BCS 2/5, weight gain 0.1 kg/day against a target of 0.35. Some coughing when moved. Temperature 38.9–39.4°C in three sampled calves. Paddock: wet lowland, grazed by the same weaner group every autumn for six years, no rotation. Dead calf: thin, with a soiled perineum.
stages.prompt: Which findings shape the differential list?

options.label: Ill-thrift with intermittent scour in weaners on repeatedly grazed ground
options.detail: Parasitic gastroenteritis in the classic setting

options.label: Coughing when the group is moved
options.detail: Lungworm alongside the gut parasites

options.label: Growth rate a third of target
options.detail: Production loss that quantifies the problem

options.label: Temperatures up to 39.4°C
options.detail: Within the range excitement produces in deer

options.label: Rough coats
options.detail: A consequence of ill-thrift, not a pointer

stages.explanation: Weaners on ground that has carried weaners every autumn for six years is the epidemiology of parasitic gastroenteritis, and the cough adds lungworm to the same picture. Growth rate is the finding that gives the farm a number to act on. Deer run hot when handled, so temperature at yarding is one of the least useful measurements you will take.

stages.title: Choose the samples
stages.briefing: The group is yarded and the dead calf is fresh enough to submit.

options.label: Individual faecal egg counts across ten calves
options.detail: Burden and its spread through the group

options.label: Faecal larval culture and Baermann for lungworm
options.detail: Speciation, and Dictyocaulus larvae

options.label: Post-mortem with total worm counts and abomasal pH
options.detail: The reference standard for deer parasitism

options.label: Serum pepsinogen with albumin and total protein
options.detail: Abomasal damage and protein loss

options.label: Trace element status — copper, cobalt and selenium
options.detail: Deficiency rides alongside ill-thrift in deer

options.label: Johne’s disease PCR on faeces as the primary test
options.detail: Worth screening later; it does not explain a six-week group problem

options.label: Bulk milk antibody testing
options.detail: These are weaned calves

stages.explanation: Deer parasitism is under-read on egg counts alone, because immature and inhibited stages produce no eggs, so the post-mortem worm count and abomasal pH are what confirm the burden. Pepsinogen and protein grade the abomasal damage, and the trace element panel is not padding in this species — copper and cobalt deficiency commonly compound the picture and change what you prescribe.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Faecal egg counts 250–1,400 epg (mean 620). Larval culture: Ostertagia-type predominant with Trichostrongylus; Baermann positive for Dictyocaulus. Post-mortem: 42,000 abomasal worms with a morocco-leather mucosa, abomasal pH 5.8 (normal 2–3), Dictyocaulus in the caudal lung lobes. Albumin 21 g/L (low), total protein 48 g/L (low), serum pepsinogen raised. Plasma copper 5.1 µmol/L (low), cobalt marginal, selenium adequate. No Johne’s lesions.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Severe parasitic gastroenteritis with abomasal damage
options.detail: 42,000 worms with an abomasal pH of 5.8 and raised pepsinogen

options.label: Concurrent lungworm infection
options.detail: Dictyocaulus on Baermann and at post-mortem

options.label: Protein-losing enteropathy from the abomasal lesions
options.detail: Albumin 21 g/L with low total protein

options.label: Copper deficiency is compounding the ill-thrift
options.detail: Plasma copper 5.1 µmol/L

options.label: Egg counts alone reflected the true burden
options.detail: A mean of 620 epg against 42,000 worms

options.label: Johne’s disease is the primary cause
options.detail: No lesions and it does not explain the worm count

stages.explanation: The gap between a mean count of 620 epg and 42,000 worms at post-mortem is the single most useful thing this submission teaches: a clinician who triaged this group on egg counts would have called the burden moderate and been badly wrong. The raised abomasal pH explains the protein loss mechanically, and the low copper is a second, separate deficit to correct.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: 42,000 abomasal worms, abomasal pH 5.8, raised pepsinogen, albumin 21 g/L, Dictyocaulus present, plasma copper 5.1 µmol/L, six years of continuous weaner grazing.

options.label: Parasitic gastroenteritis with lungworm and concurrent copper deficiency, on contaminated ground
options.detail: Both parasites, the deficiency and the reason

options.label: Johne’s disease
options.detail: No lesions, and parasitism explains the group picture

options.label: Primary copper deficiency
options.detail: Real, but secondary to a 42,000-worm burden

options.label: Yersiniosis
options.detail: An acute weaner scour, not a six-week ill-thrift with this worm count

options.label: Nutritional ill-thrift from poor pasture quality
options.detail: Does not account for the worm count or the lungworm

stages.explanation: A three-part diagnosis produces a three-part plan: an effective anthelmintic with lungworm activity now, copper supplementation checked against liver stores rather than given blindly, and a grazing rotation that stops weaners inheriting their own contamination every autumn. Naming the ground is what changes next year.
